body_markdown:
Power-hungry Americans are no strangers to the appeal of superchargers. Centrifugal Paxton superchargers made a splash on cars like the original Ford Thunderbird, while Eaton roots-type superchargers had a moment in 1989 with another winged Ford coupe. These roots-type superchargers certainly made an impact on the 2003 Cobra and a host of muscle cars that came after, but a beast came out of the blue and crashed America’s horsepower party: the AMG-tuned Mercedes-Benz E-Class, also known as the 2003-06 E55 AMG.


Or perhaps we shouldn’t have been surprised by the bruiser of a Merc, because way back in 1975 Mercedes-Benz was no stranger to impressive twist in 450SEL 6.9 guise. But a big, modern V-8 with a twin-screw blower takes that concept to the next level. The E55’s engine is known internally as the M113, and it also found homes in everything from the modest C-class sedan to the flagship SL-class roadster. The E55 AMG hit a mid-size sweet spot, though, and was stuffed with 469 horsepower and luxurious AMG thrones that are worthy of a king.


Mercedes-Benz | EVO


Mercedes-Benz | EVO


Mercedes-Benz | EVO


Even better, they made a wagon version for 193 lucky Americans back in 2005 (129 units) and 2006 (64 units). Body style aside, the E55 AMG was an unlikely entrant into the world of forced induction in the 2000s, but it ensured Mercedes-Benz had a place next to BMW’s M5 and could run with the big dogs in the American muscle car scene.


While an E55 likely got the jump on many American muscle cars in its heyday, the natural competitor is the 2003 BMW M5 (E39). With its revvy, naturally aspirated V-8 and a manual transmission, the BMW likely had a hard time keeping up with the E55 AMG and its 516 lb-ft of torque in a straight line. The subsequent 2004 E60 M5 brought a 500-hp V-10 to the fight, though it had a mere 383 lb-ft of torque.


M-B’s M113 torquey package was potent indeed, so Mercedes-Benz did the right thing by advertising the E55 AMG as “The Beast” in a memorable commercial from the otherwise milquetoast offerings you’d see on television.


Performance by the numbers was similar between the Teutonic foes, but the BMW relied on gears over grunt: its 6100-rpm torque peak likely didn’t stand a chance against the E55’s plateau from 2650 to 4000 rpm in ordinary street conditions. There was something distinctly American about how the E55 put the power down, a universal appeal for fans of big-block barnstormers and 6.9-liter Autobahn burners alike.


While the M113’s aftermarket support isn’t as robust as that of GM’s LS or Ford’s Modular V-8, you can make a real ‘bahn burner with enhancements from vendors like RENNtech and Kleemann. Be it stock or modified, there’s ample fun on tap. Now that the newest E55 AMG is 20 years old, it appears the classic car market is beginning to wise up its reputation.


Hagerty Marketplace | AGT3311


Hagerty Marketplace | AGT3311


Hagerty Marketplace | AGT3311


At least that appears to be true for this verdant E55 AMG—it remained a one-owner vehicle until this week, when it sold on[Hagerty Marketplace](https://www.hagerty.com/marketplace/auction/2005-Mercedes-Benz-E55-AMG/46bf6dec-cf05-4c47-8c8c-1ba24cbf9b59) for an impressive $48,150. This particular 2005 Mercedes-Benz E55 AMG is a rarity in the U.S. market, mostly because of its Everest Green finish and its modest 12,000-mile odometer reading. Its seller noted a 10-month wait for E55s back in 2004, but there was an opportunity to jump the line via Mercedes’ European delivery program. The seller stated it “was a no-brainer,” and this special-ordered E55 AMG began its life with a 100-mile journey on the Autobahn.


Bolstering the strong price was the fact that there are only modest flaws needing attention. There are several chips and a single scratch in the paint; it needs an “F” service, and the tires are likely too old for anything but storage. Considering the needs of cheaper, needier E55s and the parts and labor necessary to address two decades of neglect, this example’s maintenance requirements are relatively affordable and possibly even a good value.


Hagerty Marketplace | AGT3311


Hagerty Marketplace | AGT3311


Public auction sales in the last five years have about 200 examples selling for anywhere from $11,000-$40,000. Prices have remained relatively flat since 2022, but there is significant volatility due to condition—a lot of these were used as intended—countered by the E55 AMG’s relatively low production of under 8000 units from 2003-06.


The Everest Green example we are profiling here is clearly on the upper end of sales results, coming in about two grand shy of the record set for sedans in 2023. (E55 wagons, it should be noted, consistently command a premium over the sedan, and the longroof record is $64,790.) The rare color, low mileage, and single ownership history make today’s E55 an outstanding example. The Carfax report is also clean, with a relatively extensive service history at Mercedes-Benz dealerships considering the low mileage.


Considering the E55 AMG’s beast-like performance, luxurious accoutrements, and prestigious branding, prices from the last five years are unlikely to drop in the future. Depreciation is probably in this car’s rearview mirror, and it’s faring quite well compared to its nearest *supercharged* counterpart, the 2003-2004 “Terminator” Mustang Cobra. We[recently noted](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/why-on-earth-are-sn95-mustangs-slept-on-by-enthusiasts/#:~:text=That%20story%20unfolds%20as%20the%20Terminator%20Cobra%20coupe%20is%20valued%20at%20%2434%2C100%20in%20%232%20condition%2C%20slightly%20lower%20at%20%2432%2C900%20for%20the%20convertible.) that this supercharged V-8 Mustang is valued at $34,100 in #2 condition, which is likely lower than a comparable E55 AMG by several thousand dollars.


Of course, the more logical comparison is to the E60 BMW M5, which ranges from $39,800 to $67,667 in #2 condition over the past five years. The M-series has its performance benefits, especially outside of straight-line acceleration, and that’s likely one reason why it is worth more than the E55 AMG. But those numbers might be misleading, as the Hagerty Valuation Team notes a 50% premium for models equipped with a manual transmission. Factor that into the equation, and the automatic-equipped BMW M5s are more neck-and-neck with the E55 AMG. (Besides,[manual transmission sales](https://web.archive.org/web/20180228104746/http://www.m5portal.com/forum/e60m5_nb93_2ma.asp) were well under 20% of total E60 M5 sales in America.)


Maybe history is repeating itself, as the E55 AMG proves there’s inherent appeal in a supercharged V-8 wrapped in a luxurious Mercedes-Benz body. It may not have the same appeal as a manual-transmission V-10 M5, but even BMW’s finest better not get caught napping in the wrong gear. This “Beast” is bound to “Terminate” its competition for the foreseeable future.
